My understanding of Axis 👇🏻

https://t.co/3Njr6D1MVx

https://t.co/N8dXTm7WBw

The easiest way I see Axis is:

> Axis is trying to build the data layer that Physical AI is missing.

Everyone talks about better robot models.

But a model is only as good as the experiences it learns from.

And physical world experience is extremely difficult to collect.

A human can learn how to pick up a glass after seeing thousands of slightly different situations.

A robot needs those experiences represented as data.

That's the bottleneck Axis is attacking.

1. The real opportunity isn't “robot simulation”

This is where I would differentiate your content.

If you say:

> “Axis is building a robotics simulator.”

You're technically describing part of it, but you're missing the bigger picture.

The simulator is the environment where the data can be produced.

The actual product thesis is much bigger:

Create → collect → improve → train → deploy → observe failure → correct → retrain

That is the engine.

The simulator is one component of that engine.

2. Think about how AI developed

Text AI had the internet.

Billions of pages.

Images.

Videos.

Code.

Human conversations.

That gave AI an enormous learning resource.

Robotics doesn't have an equivalent universal dataset.

There isn't a giant database containing:

> “Here are 500 million examples of humans successfully manipulating objects in every possible environment.”

And even if there were, robots don't just need visual information.

They need action data.

They need to learn:

What should I do?

How should I move?

What happens if I move incorrectly?

How do I recover?

That's why robotics data is fundamentally different from ordinary AI data.

3. Axis turns people into a distributed data collection network

This is one of the strongest ideas behind the project.

Imagine you have 10 robotics researchers.

They can only collect so much data.

Now imagine 10,000 people around the world can contribute through a browser.

The hardware requirement disappears for the contributor.

No robot laboratory.

No expensive robot arm.

No specialized robotics setup.

People can generate simulated robot experiences.

That changes the economics of data collection.

And this is where Axis becomes interesting from a network perspective.

It's not just:

Company builds dataset.

It's potentially:

Network produces dataset.

4. But human data alone isn't enough

Here's another important point.

Suppose 1,000 people perform the same task.

You don't necessarily get 1,000 useful variations.

Maybe everyone performs it almost identically.

Robots need diversity.

So simulation becomes extremely useful.

You can vary:

object location

environment

camera

lighting

physical parameters

object properties

task conditions

Now the system can take relatively limited human demonstrations and generate broader training scenarios.

So I wouldn't describe Axis as:

> “Humans create data.”

I'd describe it as:

> Humans provide real behavioral signals and simulation provides scale and diversity.

That combination is much more powerful

5. Then comes the really interesting part: V2

This is probably the most important concept for you to understand.

V1 is basically:

Human → Robot demonstration

The human teaches.

V2 changes the relationship:

AI → attempts task → human watches → intervention when necessary

Now the human doesn't have to do everything.

The AI does the easy parts itself.

The human focuses on mistakes.

And that's valuable.

Because the hardest examples aren't necessarily successful demonstrations.

Sometimes the most useful information is:

> “The model tried this and failed here. This is what it should have done instead.”

That's why post-training data can become extremely valuable.

6. Think of V2 as a teacher correcting a student

Imagine a student solving a problem.

You don't need to solve every problem for them.

You let them try.

When they're wrong:

stop → explain the mistake → show the correct approach → let them continue.

That's essentially the intuition behind the human gated correction loop.

For robotics:

Policy attempts

↓

Policy makes mistake

↓

Human intervenes

↓

Correct behavior recorded

↓

Training signal created

↓

Next policy becomes better

↓

New policy attempts more difficult situations

This is why the word compounding matters.

The system isn't just accumulating raw data.

It is trying to accumulate better and more targeted data

7. And this could solve a huge robotics problem

Robots are often good at very specific controlled tasks.

But the real world is messy.

A robot trained to pick up one object on one table doesn't automatically become good at picking up every object everywhere.

Generalization is difficult.

Axis's approach is essentially:

> Give the model more environments, more embodiments, more tasks, more variations and more corrections.

The ambition is to move from:

robot knows one task

towards:

robot learns transferable skills.

That's a much harder problem.

And it's also where the biggest potential value is.

8. The sim to real part is where you should stay realistic

Don't oversell this.

Simulation is powerful.

But simulation isn't reality.

A simulator can never perfectly reproduce every detail of the physical world.

There will always be:

sensor noise

friction differences

imperfect physics

unexpected objects

hardware limitations

environmental changes

So Axis has to solve the sim-to-real gap.

The important thing is that the project has already reported early real robot validation.

The “Little Prince's Rose” experiment is particularly interesting because Axis reported collecting 10,000+ trajectories through browser-based contribution, training a policy from that data, and deploying it on a real robot for the task.

That doesn't mean the general robotics problem is solved.

It means the basic pipeline has been demonstrated.

And that's the correct way to present it.

9. Here's where I see the biggest long term opportunity

If Axis succeeds, the valuable thing may not be the individual simulation task.

It could be the dataset and feedback infrastructure around Physical AI.

Think about what happens if the network becomes large:

More contributors

→ more demonstrations

→ more task diversity

→ larger datasets

→ better policies

→ more real-world deployments

→ more failures discovered

→ more correction data

→ better policies again

That creates a potential data flywheel.

And data flywheels are extremely difficult for competitors to reproduce once they become large.

Because the advantage isn't just software.

It's:

data + contributors + models + feedback + provenance.

10. Now the crypto side makes more sense

I wouldn't make crypto the headline.

I'd make it the coordination layer.

Because once thousands or millions of people contribute data, new questions appear:

Who created this data?

When was it created?

Which task produced it?

Was it accepted?

Was it used?

Can the contribution be verified?

Who should receive credit?

This is where on chain provenance can become useful.

Axis says accepted trajectories can receive unique Data IDs and provenance records on Base.

So the interesting idea isn't:

> “They added blockchain because Web3.”

It's:

> If data becomes an economic asset, you need a way to track its origin and contribution history

That's a much stronger explanation.

11. Points are not the whole story

This is something I'd strongly recommend you keep in mind when making posts.

Don't reduce Axis to:

“Do tasks → earn Points → wait for airdrop.”

That's the weakest possible narrative.

The better narrative is:

Your contribution creates a robotics data asset.

Points are currently the incentive mechanism.

Axis has said Points may be one input into a future Community Contributor Airdrop, but final terms are not guaranteed.

So you should never tell people:

> “Do 1,000 tasks and you'll get X.”

Instead say:

> Contributions are currently tracked through Points and Axis has indicated that Points may factor into a future contributor distribution

That's accurate and safer.

12. What I would personally focus on if I were creating Axis content

I'd build around five themes.

Theme 1 — The Physical AI data problem

Explain why robots don't have the same data advantage as language models.

Theme 2 — Browser → Robot data

Explain how an ordinary person can contribute useful robot experiences without owning hardware.

Theme 3 — V2 / Human correction

This is probably the strongest technical story.

AI makes mistakes.

Humans correct those mistakes.

Those corrections improve future policies.

Theme 4 — Sim-to-real

Explain why simulation matters and why getting simulated skills onto physical robots is difficult.

Theme 5 — Data ownership + provenance

Explain why blockchain can potentially become useful when thousands of people contribute valuable AI training data.

13. And what should YOU actually do?

If your goal is to participate seriously rather than just farm:

First

Understand the difference between Pre-training and Post-training.

Second

Complete tasks carefully.

Don't assume faster = better.

Third

Pay attention to mistakes.

Especially in Postntraining.

The correction you're providing is potentially more informative than simply completing an easy task.

Fourth

Keep track of your contribution history and Points.

Fifth

Participate in the community.

Feedback, bug reports, helping new contributors and useful observations can also matter to the ecosystem.

Sixth

Create educational content around what you're actually learning.

Don't copy Axis's announcements.

Instead explain:

> Why does this matter?

That's where your content becomes original.

14. The biggest thing I learned about Axis

Before researching it, it would be easy to see Axis as:

robot simulator + points + crypto

After looking at the architecture, I think that's too shallow.

The better mental model is:

Axis = a distributed data pipeline for Physical AI

The simulator gives robots a scalable environment.

Humans provide behavioral demonstrations.

Data processing and augmentation increase diversity.

Models learn from those experiences.

V2 lets models generate their own attempts.

Humans correct failures.

Those corrections become new training data.

Blockchain can provide provenance and contributor coordination.

And the long-term objective is to make the whole thing continuously improve.

That's the actual story.

One sentence I'd keep in your head

> Axis isn't trying to make humans play with virtual robots. It's trying to turn human interaction and simulation into a continuously improving training infrastructure for physical machines

COMPLETE STEP-BY-STEP: CREATE YOUR FIRST AI UGC AD
THE PROJECT WE'RE CREATING

We are going to create a complete AI UGC advertisement for a skincare product. We are starting with nothing no character, no voice, no images, no video. By the end, we will have a finished UGC ad.

Our production pipeline will be:

Product → Research → Script → Character → Character Sheet → Voice → Storyboard → Images → Video → Editing → Sound → Final Ad.

Incase you don't know what those terms are; they are the full workflow to make our ad. 

Here’s what each term means:

1. Product: 
This is what we are creating the UGC Ad to talk about. 

Example: A skincare cream.

Without this, we have no ad.

2. Research
We need to understand the product + audience + competitors. 

What pain does it solve? What hook will stop people scrolling? Etc

3. Script
The words + story for our ad.

We need a: Hook → Problem → Solution → CTA.

Here is a simple Example: "Tired of acne? This cream cleared my skin in 7 days. Shop now"

4. Character
Who is in the ad? The face/person that will sell it.

Example: "Beautiful black woman, 28, confident, in bathroom

5. Character Sheet
This is the reference file of that character. Outfit, face, hairstyle, expression.

This keeps the AI from changing her face in every scene so can have Consistency.

6. Voice
The voiceover/voice clone you’ll use.
Example: Nigerian female voice, aged 33, friendly, fast. 

7. Storyboard
This will break down the ad into 
 shots. Like a comic strip.

For example:

Shot 1: Hook - close up of acne. Shot 2: Apply cream. 
Shot 3: Clear skin + product + CTA.

The story board will plan the visuals before we generate.

8. Image
We need to generate the key frames for each storyboard shot using and image generator eg Midjourney, Grok, Nano Banana etc

These images are the "scenes" of our ad.

9. Video
After creation, we would turn those images into motion. You can use Kling, Veo3, Runway, Pika, Seedance etc.

You will add the  camera movement, expressions, dialogue etc.

10. Editing
Finally we, Cut everything together in CapCut/Premiere. 

We will add  cuts, zooms, text-on-screen, captions, pacing. This is where ads become scroll-stoppers.

11. Sound
Here, we add background music, sound effects, and mix the voiceover.

For Example: We could use a trending TikTok sound + whoosh SFX when product appears.

12. Final Ad.
Export the video.

Now it’s ready to run as a Facebook/YouTube ad.

For this creation, we would be using Google Flow to Generate our Ads.

The emergence of procedural world generation from textual prompts, as demonstrated in applications rendering narrative environments from literary sources, highlights a significant threshold in generative modeling. This capability moves beyond static image or text creation into the synthesis of dynamic, interactive systems. Karpathy's observation of a large language model orchestrating polygonal assets in 3D space from a high-level description aligns with research in grounded language acquisition, where symbolic representations must be mapped to sensory or simulated environments.

This process can be framed within the context of "program synthesis," a field that has seen substantial progress with models like AlphaCode. However, the task here is complex, involving the translation of abstract narrative concepts ("a party of special magnificence") into concrete spatial and temporal arrangements. The "jank" or error in the output, as noted, underscores the grounding problem: the model's capacity to generate syntactically correct code for a renderer exists alongside a limited ability to "perceive" or internally validate the resulting visual-kinematic experience.

This limitation points to a core area of research in embodied AI. Work by researchers like Jitendra Malik and colleagues on learning from video and interaction suggests that models require feedback loops that are more integrated than textual or static image-based supervision. An LLM's inability to "play the game" it has created is analogous to a lack of proprioceptive or visual feedback, a challenge that work in reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) and simulation-to-real transfer attempts to address. The potential for "ephemeral GTA of X on demand" is contingent on solving this validation and iteration cycle, likely through multimodal architectures that can process video or interactive state data as natively as they process text.

Tarun on how AI training evolved from pre-training to self generating harnesses and why data costs are catching up to compute

"Let's take a tiny history lesson. In 2023, with stable diffusion and GPT-3, it was just bigger is better, pre-training. Then in 2024 it was directed RL, how you feed the data after training, this in context learning type of stuff, which got you another order of magnitude performance increase across a lot of evals and practical use cases"

"Then the harness thing was, if you customize how you do the RL for different applications, you get even better performance versus a generic RL environment. And the current meta-harness, the generic can answer anything, Claude Code or Codex type of thing, which arguably is what killed Cursor and why I'd argue they ended up doing the acquisition, that can figure out which environment to use just in time"

"The problem with this environment stuff from a data consumption perspective is you now have to pay a lot more for annotated data to customize the different environments. That's why people have been talking about data cost coming close to matching compute cost for training, because you need much more annotated data for each specific task domain"

"The belief is that once one of these things is good enough, instead of having to get data this way and generating synthetic data via RL, the model can generate the harness in real time"

The same problem resurfaces in LLM evaluation. A benchmark score gets read as a direct measure of capability, but it is an aggregate over items that are not interchangeable instruments.

Zhou et al. fit an item response model to 41,871 items across 11 benchmarks and estimated difficulty, discriminability, guessing rate, and feasibility for each one. The aggregate conceals how uneven these are. Some items have discriminability near zero and separate nothing. Some carry guessing rates above 0.75, which the authors read as a contamination signal. Estimated item difficulty rarely exceeds 1.0 while the strongest models sit above 3.0. TheoremQA averages 0.50 on feasibility, so many of its questions cannot be answered from what they supply.

The cost is measurable. Among the stronger models, 1,000 items selected for Fisher information reproduced the human-preference ranking at Kendall's τ of 0.90, while the full pooled set managed 0.24. More items made the ranking worse. The question is not who scored higher on accuracy, but who was separated by items capable of separating anything. 8/9
